newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan opposition says Pakistan helping Taleban.
newsitem.headline: Afghan opposition says Pakistan helping Taleban.

text.p: MAZAR-I-SHARIF, Afghanistan, June 10 (Reuturs) - A senior official of the ousted Afghan government reiterated accusations of Pakistani backing for the purist Islamic Taleban militia which now rules more than two thirds of Afghanistan.
Abdul Rahim Ghafoorzai told a news conference on Monday night that Islamabad was helping the Taleban recruit new fighters among pupils at Islamic religious schools in Pakistan.

"We have documentary evidence that the Pakistanis are involved in the recruitment of thousands of militias for the Taleban," he said in the northern opposition stronghold of Mazar-i-Sharif. He did not produce the evidence.
Witnesses in Pakistan and Afghanistan say thousands of Taleban recruits have crossed the border since the Taleban were kicked out of Mazar-i-Sharif on May 28 in a humiliating debacle.
Ghafoorzai was deputy foreign minister in ousted president Burhanuddin Rabbani's government, which the Taleban drove from Kabul when they captured the Afghan capital on September 27.
He said the Pakistani Jamaat-i-Islami party was particularly active in the recruitment campaign.
"We cannot accept that the Pakistani authorities are completely unaware of this process," Ghafoorzai said.
Pakistan denies supporting the Taleban, but is widely seen as the militia's best foreign friend, becoming the first country formally to recognise the Taleban government in Kabul on May 25.
Ghafoorzai voiced concern that Pakistan might take a direct role in the Afghan conflict after recent reverses suffered by the Taleban in northern Afghanistan.
"In the light of widespread (Taleban) defeats, I think that there is clear concern...that the Pakistani authorities may openly get involved in the Afghan conflict," he said.
Ghafoorzai rejected Taleban accusations that opposition factions were receiving military assistance from neighbouring Central Asian states, particularly Tajikistan.

On Sunday, Taleban Deputy Foreign Minister Sher Abbas Stanakzai said in Kabul that a military helicopter had ferried weapons from Tajikistan's southern Kulyab province to opposition bases in Afghanistan before its pilots defected to the Taleban.
"There are some military flights going to Kulyab to take wounded for treatment, but I have no idea of any military assistance coming from Kulyab," Ghafoorzai said.
He urged Uzbekistan to increase cooperation with the anti-Taleban alliance in the north.

Uzbekistan, alarmed at seeing the Taleban close to its territory, closed its border with Afghanistan after an opposition commander made a short-lived pact with the Taleban that allowed them to move into the north last month.
But the agreement collapsed and the Taleban were driven out of Mazar-i-Sharif after losing at least 300 dead.
Uzbekistan is believed to be uneasy at the fate of former opposition leader General Abdul Rashid Dostum, who was forced into exile in Turkey by a mutiny led by General Abdul Malik.
Malik has replaced Dostum, who had close relations with Uzbekistan, at the head of the opposition Junbish-i-Milli faction that controls about six northern provinces.
"Uzbekistan should not feel concerned," Ghafoorzai said, urging Tashkent to cooperate with Junbish-i-Milli.
Ghafoorzai reiterated longstanding opposition demands for a ceasefire and de-militarisation of Kabul as prerequisites for a negotiated peace and formation of a broad-based government.
"We still believe that the military solution is not the advisable way to solve the problem in Afghanistan," he said.
"There will be a gradual release of prisoners of war, but only after the Taleban agree to accept the capital as a de-militarised city," he added.
A Taleban spokesman said the movement was willing to hold talks with Malik, but wanted him to prove his sincerity by freeing Taleban prisoners captured in Mazar-i-Sharif.
The International Committee of the Red Cross said it knew of 700 prisoners in Mazar-i-Sharif after the Taleban defeat.
